analysis.one_liner: Banned states from sponsoring or licensing sports betting, preserving Nevada's legal sportsbook monopoly.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate 88-5, cleared the House by voice vote, and became Public Law 102-559 when the President signed it on October 28, 1992.
analysis.plain_summary: This law makes it illegal for any state or local government to operate, sponsor, advertise, promote, license, or authorize betting on professional or amateur sports, with a few exceptions for states that already had schemes in place. It was sold as protecting the integrity of games from state-run gambling. In practice, it froze legal sports betting in place: Nevada's licensed sportsbooks kept a national monopoly, and everyone else who wanted to bet had to use illegal or offshore bookies, with no state able to legalize, regulate, or tax the market for 26 years until the Supreme Court struck the law down in 2018.
analysis.who_benefits: Professional and amateur sports leagues got a federal shield: no state could license betting on their games, and the law lets them sue in federal court to stop states that try. Nevada's licensed sportsbooks kept the only legal sports betting market in the country. Offshore and illegal bookmakers also benefited, since demand for betting did not go away — it just moved to unregulated markets.

how_it_helps.text: The law makes it unlawful for a governmental entity, or a person acting under its law, to operate, sponsor, advertise, promote, license, or authorize a lottery, sweepstakes, or other betting scheme based on professional or amateur sports games or performances. [S3] [S5]
It gives leagues a private enforcement tool: any party may bring a civil action in federal district court to enjoin a state's sports betting scheme. [S3] [S5]

For Nevada's casinos, the bill's final version carved out specified exceptions that grandfathered existing schemes, preserving the state's licensed sportsbooks as the nation's only legal sports betting market. [S4] [S5]

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, ordinary bettors in 49 states bear the cost: no legal, regulated, taxed sports betting anywhere outside Nevada, so wagering money flows to illegal bookmakers and offshore sites with no consumer protections and no tax revenue for states. State lotteries and treasuries also lose a potential revenue source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bettors and state governments outside Nevada

drawbacks.text: The ban pushes sports wagering into unregulated markets: betting demand does not disappear, so money moves to illegal bookies and offshore operators with no licensing, no dispute resolution, and no tax revenue for states. [S5]

It overrides state authority: a state that wanted to legalize and tax sports betting — as several later attempted — cannot, and the final version's exceptions protect existing schemes in a few states while locking everyone else out. [S4] [S5]

The strongest good-faith objection to those drawbacks, as supporters argued, is that state-sponsored betting on games risks fixing and undermines the integrity of amateur and professional sports, which the federal ban guards against. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is one-directional: it gives leagues a federal veto over state betting policy and entrenches Nevada's monopoly, while doing nothing to regulate or tax the betting that continues elsewhere. Whatever integrity benefit it provides could have been achieved by regulating betting rather than banning it everywhere but Nevada, and the 2018 Supreme Court decision that voided the law reflected how lopsended the arrangement was. The costs fell on bettors and state treasuries for a quarter-century.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with a report and minority views, passed the Senate 88-5, passed the House by voice vote under a suspension of the rules (a fast-track procedure with limited debate), and was signed by the President on October 28, 1992 as Public Law 102-559.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator DeConcini on February 22, 1991, the bill would have barred states from sponsoring, operating, advertising, authorizing, licensing, or promoting any betting scheme based on professional or amateur sports. [S1] [S2]
It had 63 Senate cosponsors — 34 Republicans and 29 Democrats — showing broad bipartisan support from the start. [S6]
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings, approved it in subcommittee, and reported it favorably with a substitute amendment on November 26, 1991, with minority views filed. [S3] [S7]
The Senate passed it 88-5 on June 2, 1992, with Democrats voting 53-2 and Republicans 35-3 in favor. [S8]

The House passed it by voice vote on October 6, 1992 under suspension of the rules, the Senate agreed to the House amendments the next day, and the President signed it on October 28, 1992, making it Public Law 102-559. [S5] [S7]
The final version set forth specified exceptions to the ban, preserving existing schemes — notably Nevada's licensed sports betting — while barring new ones elsewhere. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Professional sports leagues and Nevada's licensed sportsbooks came out ahead: the leagues got a federal ban on state betting and a right to sue states, and Nevada kept the only legal sports betting market in America for the next 26 years.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: the Senate passed it 88-5 with Democrats at 53-2 and Republicans at 35-3, and it had 63 cosponsors split 34 Republicans and 29 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill hands the leagues a federal ban on state-licensed betting on their games plus a private right to sue states that try. Their gain came directly at the cost of bettors and states that might otherwise have legalized and taxed betting.

The final version's exceptions grandfathered existing schemes, making Nevada's sportsbooks the permanent legal channel for sports betting nationwide. Anyone else who wanted to bet legally had to travel or use Nevada-based books.
With legal betting confined to Nevada, demand elsewhere flowed to unregulated bookies and offshore sites that the law could not reach — no consumer protections, no taxes.
States were barred from sponsoring, licensing, or authorizing sports betting, cutting off a potential revenue source; several states later challenged the law in court.
